mcqs.question: What is the recommended rule of thumb for when to split a class along SRP lines?
options: Split as soon as a class has more than three methods, regardless of what they do
Never split unless a senior engineer explicitly requests it in review
Split when you can name two actual, currently-happening reasons the class changes for different actors
Split only after the class has caused a production incident
mcqs.explanation: The useful threshold is real, present change driven by distinct actors — not a method count, an incident history, or waiting for someone to ask. Splitting preemptively for a reason that hasn't shown up yet just adds navigation cost with no current benefit.

mcqs.question: A `UserOnboarding` class validates, normalizes, saves, and notifies for a new user, all changing together for the same reason today. Why is keeping this as one class the right call?
options: One class is always correct regardless of how the steps change over time
The four steps currently change together for the same reason, so splitting would add navigation cost without isolating any real independent change yet
SRP doesn't apply to onboarding flows specifically
Splitting is only valid once the class exceeds 100 lines of code
mcqs.explanation: The deciding factor is whether the steps actually vary independently — while they don't, one file to understand the whole flow beats four files with no isolation benefit. There's no onboarding-specific exemption and no universal line-count threshold; the right call depends on real, current change patterns.

mcqs.question: How can a class satisfy SRP (one reason to change) while still failing cohesion?
options: This is impossible — satisfying SRP guarantees cohesion automatically
SRP only applies to classes, while cohesion only applies to modules, so they can't be compared
Cohesion is just another name for SRP, so the question doesn't make sense
A class can have exactly one reason to change while its methods still don't share data or purpose beyond that single narrow reason, making it individually single-purpose but scattered
mcqs.explanation: SRP and cohesion measure different things — one reason to change doesn't guarantee the methods belong together in any deeper sense. Over-applying SRP without checking cohesion produces classes that are technically single-purpose but force callers to juggle many scattered pieces. They aren't the same concept, and both can apply at class or module granularity.

mcqs.question: Why is "SRP is overrated, keep everything in one class" the wrong overcorrection?
options: It throws away SRP's real benefit once a class genuinely serves multiple actors — merge conflicts, blast-radius risk, and untestable god-classes are real costs of not splitting
It is correct — SRP has no real benefit in any codebase size
It's wrong only for functional languages, not object-oriented ones
It's wrong because every class must have exactly one public method to be maintainable
mcqs.explanation: SRP's benefits are real once multiple actors are actually driving change through the same class — refusing to split ever ignores that cost. The right answer isn't picking either extreme, it's naming where the trade-off flips. There's no language-specific exemption or method-count rule involved.
